title: What are the challenges of sharding: cross-shard queries/joins (scatter-gather, expensive), cross-shard transactions (2PC or Saga), resharding/rebalancing when adding nodes, maintaining referential integrity, schema migrations across shards, and operational complexity?
keyPoints: Cross-shard queries and joins require scatter-gather across all shards and lose the single-node optimizer.
Cross-shard transactions need two-phase commit (blocking, coordinator failure risk) or Saga patterns with compensating actions.
Resharding and rebalancing when adding nodes requires online data movement; consistent hashing limits movement to roughly 1/N of keys.
Foreign keys cannot cross shards, so referential integrity becomes an application responsibility with background reconciliation.
Schema migrations must be coordinated across every shard, rolled out in backward-compatible waves with version tracking.
Operational complexity multiplies: more nodes mean more monitoring, backups per shard, consistent configuration, and harder debugging.
The senior principle is to not shard prematurely: exhaust vertical scaling, read replicas, and caching first because sharding's complexity is permanent.

s1_definition.oneliner: Sharding buys scale but charges you in cross-shard queries, distributed transactions, resharding, lost foreign keys, coordinated migrations, and operational complexity.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Cross-shard queries** – Queries spanning shards require scatter-gather fan-out and lose the single-node optimizer, getting slower as shard count grows.
- **Cross-shard transactions** – Atomic changes across shards need two-phase commit or Saga patterns with compensating actions.
- **Resharding** – Adding nodes forces data movement; naive modulo reshuffles everything, consistent hashing limits it to ~1/N.
- **Lost referential integrity** – Foreign keys cannot cross shards, so constraints become application responsibilities.
- **Coordinated migrations** – Every shard must receive identical schema changes, rolled out in waves.
- **Operational complexity** – More nodes mean more monitoring, backups, configuration, and debugging.
s1_definition.analogy: Once National Bank of India spreads accounts across many branches, a report covering all customers must ask every branch and stitch the answers together. A transfer between two customers in different branches needs both branches to agree atomically. Adding a new branch means physically moving some accounts. And a form change must be rolled out to every branch identically. The bank gains scale but pays in coordination.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sharding buys horizontal scale but introduces real distributed-systems challenges that are permanent. Queries and joins not confined to one shard must scatter-gather across all shards and merge in the application, losing the single-node optimizer. Atomic changes across shards need two-phase commit or a Saga of local transactions with compensating actions: the debit happens on one shard, the credit on another, and if the credit fails, a compensation action reverses the debit. Adding nodes forces resharding, so consistent hashing with virtual nodes limits data movement to roughly 1/N of the keys.

Foreign keys cannot cross shards, so referential integrity moves into the application with background reconciliation. Schema migrations must be rolled out in backward-compatible waves to every shard with version tracking. And the whole system is operationally heavier: more nodes to monitor, back up, patch, and debug.

The best mitigation is co-locating related data on the same shard. If Rajesh's customer record, accounts, and transactions all live on the same shard, most operations stay local. Only cross-customer transfers need the Saga pattern.

At the National Bank of India, a bank-wide total balance report scatter-gathers a SUM from every shard and adds them in the coordinator. A transfer between Rajesh on one shard and Priya on another runs as a Saga: debit first, then credit, with a compensating re-credit if the credit fails. The principle Pankaj always states is to not shard prematurely: exhaust vertical scaling, replicas, and caching first, because once data is sharded the coordination cost is permanent.

Remember one sentence: sharding charges you in cross-shard queries, distributed transactions, resharding, lost foreign keys, coordinated migrations, and operational complexity.
